Issued at 230 AM CDT Mon Oct 26 2026

Soggy Start to the Week...It's a cool and dreary start to the work 
week across the Upper Midwest. 2 AM MPX radar imagery captured a 
slow-moving batch of showers across central MN and another area of 
showers moving east of the MN River between Redwood Falls and 
Mankato. Precipitation rates remain light with this activity and a 
slight decrease in coverage over the coming hours is likely for
at least central MN as an embedded wave supporting this round 
of precipitation drifts east into central WI. The national radar
displays rain showers and a few thunderstorms extending from 
the northern Great Plains all the way to portions of NM, TX, & 
OK. Precipitation can be seen lifting north along a baroclinic 
zone that has setup between an upper-low pivoting northeast of 
the Four Corners region and a strong ridge over the eastern half
of the CONUS. Aforementioned baroclinic gradient serves as the 
"track" for widespread precipitation as the upper-low lifts 
north across NE and the Dakotas later today. A broad precipitation
shield, supported by isentropic ascent, anomalous PWATs, and a 
strengthening mid-level temperature gradient will spread north 
with time from mid-morning onward. Rainfall rates will gradually
increase with the approach of an associated surface low, along
with a stronger punch of omega forcing. It's expected that the 
heaviest rates won't move into the forecast area until later 
this afternoon, starting across southwestern MN and expanding 
northeastward. Rain will continue into tonight prior to 
diminishing by daybreak Tuesday as the precipitation shield 
exits to the north. Cloud cover, persistent rain, and light 
northeasterly flow will really limit warming and result in 
widespread highs in the 40s. Locations near I-90 and farther 
east into western WI have the best chance of warming into the 
lower 50s. 

Rainfall Expectations...As discussed by yesterday's dayshift, there 
was a slight eastward shift in the heaviest rainfall footprint, 
which brings the potential for 1"+ amounts a bit farther east into 
portions of central and western MN (consensus heaviest rainfall 
swath extends from Sioux Falls to Redwood Falls to St. Cloud). 
Despite the shift, the corridor will still be relatively narrow and 
amounts will drop off to the east of this line. Latest precipitation 
probabilities for exceeding a half inch of rain are: 80-90% at 
Madison, Redwood Falls, Alexandria & St. Cloud, 50-60% at Mankato & 
across the Twin Cities Metro and less than 20% at Red Wing, & Eau 
Claire. Latest hi-res blends (REFS/HREF) advertise a notable QPF 
gradient across the Twin Cities Metro (from northwest to southeast). 

Rest of the Week/Upcoming Weekend...Rain ends by/just after daybreak 
on Tuesday and focus will turn towards the next upper-low set to 
advance across the northern CONUS within broad southwesterly flow 
aloft. Majority of the precipitation associated with this feature 
will remain well to the north and west of the forecast area. 
However, the advection of a warmer air mass in advance of the 
feature will bring a notably warmer day with highs ranging from the 
mid-50s across west central MN to the mid 60s across eastern MN and 
western WI. WAA continues into Wednesday, which should yield the 
warmest day of the work week with highs in the upper 60s to lower 
70s. Guidance is coming into better agreement with the handling of a 
cold frontal passage later Wednesday into Thursday. The potentially 
warmer pre-frontal air mass will feature a narrow plume of
instability supportive of showers and scattered thunderstorms 
Wednesday evening. The front will sag to the south of the 
forecast area on Thursday, allowing for a dry and slightly 
cooler day. Forecast confidence decreases Friday onward as an 
active western split-flow regime sends a series of waves 
towards the central portion of the country. Over the past few 
days we've talked about Friday as potentially being a warm day, 
but the latest trends in the guidance have muddied the waters 
somewhat owing to significant timing disparities between large 
scale features. With this in mind, I like that the NBM has 
pulled back slightly, while still running above normal with 
highs in the lower 60s Friday through the upcoming weekend. 
Nearly all members of global ensembles and machine learning 
counterparts feature measurable precipitation during the 
upcoming weekend -- once again, it's a matter of timing given 
the evolution of the upper features. We'll continue to roll with
chance PoPs on Halloween given the ensemble trends, but will 
need a few days to have a better handle on timing and coverage.
